title: Erikson's Life Stages
objective: After this level you can explain Erik Erikson's stages of development from infancy to old age.
summary: Erik Erikson turned Freud's childhood theory into eight psychosocial stages across the whole lifespan, each with its own task, from trust in infancy to integrity in old age.

cards.headline: Freud thought personality was shaped in childhood. Erikson kept going.
cards.body: Erik Erikson took Freud's theory and stretched it across the whole of life. In his view, every age brings its own big task, from a baby learning to trust to an older adult looking back. Which one are you working on now?

cards.headline: Social, and lifelong
cards.body: Erikson turned Freud's ideas into a psychosocial theory: how we interact with other people shapes our sense of self. And where Freud believed personality is shaped only in childhood, Erikson said it keeps developing across the lifespan. He described eight stages from infancy to late adulthood. Each has a conflict or task to work through, and resolving it brings a sense of competence.

events.label: Trust vs. mistrust: responsive care makes the world feel safe
Identity vs. role confusion: "Who am I?"
Intimacy vs. isolation: building close relationships
Generativity vs. stagnation: contributing to others
Integrity vs. despair: looking back on a life

cards.headline: The tasks of adulthood
cards.body: Three of the eight stages belong to adults. Intimacy comes first, and Erikson said it needs a strong sense of self. Generativity means finding your life's work and contributing to others, through volunteering, mentoring or raising children. Integrity versus despair closes the list: looking back on life with a sense of satisfaction, or of failure. Growing up, for Erikson, never quite finishes.

mascot.line: You don't need every age range. Remember the arc: trust in infancy, identity in adolescence, integrity in late life.

cards.headline: Erikson's life stages
learned: Erikson made development social and lifelong
Eight stages, each with a task
From trust in infancy to integrity in late adulthood

questions.prompt: In Erikson's theory, what is the task of late adulthood?

options.label: Trust versus mistrust
options.rationale: That is the task of infancy.

options.label: Identity versus role confusion
options.rationale: That is the task of adolescence.

options.label: Generativity versus stagnation
options.rationale: That is the task of middle adulthood.

questions.explanation: In late adulthood, people look back on their lives with satisfaction or a sense of failure: integrity versus despair.

questions.prompt: How does Erikson's view of personality development differ from Freud's?

options.label: It keeps developing across the whole lifespan
It is complete by the age of 5
options.rationale: That is closer to Freud's view that childhood shapes personality.

options.label: It depends only on rewards and punishments
It is fixed by genes at birth
options.rationale: Erikson stressed social interaction, not fixed genes.

questions.explanation: Freud believed personality is shaped only in childhood; Erikson said it develops across the lifespan.

questions.prompt: Level 4 said research supports Freud's broad idea that childhood experience helps shape personality. How does Erikson build on it?

options.label: He rejects childhood as unimportant
options.rationale: His first stages are in infancy and childhood.

options.label: He adds stages that continue through adulthood
He limits development to the first year of life
options.rationale: He described eight stages, to late adulthood.

questions.explanation: Erikson kept childhood's importance but said development continues across the lifespan, in eight stages.
